core: The scientific method as the systematic process of asking questions and testing answers with evidence
The commonly taught steps: question, hypothesis, test, analyze, conclude, share (and repeat)
Hypotheses as testable, falsifiable predictions; good versus vague hypotheses
Why psychology needs the method: the mind is hard to study and intuition is unreliable (confirmation bias)
Replication: results must hold when a study is repeated
The honest note: science is self-correcting, not perfect
supporting: Empirical knowledge as the hallmark of scientific evidence
Falsifiability as a requirement for a scientific hypothesis
The distinction between a hypothesis and a theory
Facts versus opinions in the scientific community
outOfScope: Specific research designs and methods (own sibling topic: research-methods)
Experiments and experimental design details (own sibling topic: experiments)
What psychology studies as a discipline (own sibling topic: what-psychology-studies)

claims.claim: The scientific method is the process by which scientific knowledge advances: ideas in the form of theories and hypotheses are tested against the real world in the form of empirical observations, and those observations lead to more ideas that are tested in turn.
A hypothesis is a testable prediction about how the world will behave if the researcher's idea is correct, often worded as an if-then statement.

A good scientific hypothesis must be falsifiable — capable of being shown to be incorrect — and testable, rather than vague; a claim that cannot be contradicted by any observation cannot be tested scientifically.

The method is commonly taught as a cycle of steps: make an observation, ask a question, form a hypothesis, test it by gathering data, analyze the data and draw conclusions, share the results, and repeat; the steps are guidelines rather than a rigid fixed sequence.

Scientific knowledge is empirical: grounded in objective, tangible evidence that can be observed time and time again, regardless of who is observing, rather than in intuition, authority, or personal experience alone.

Confirmation bias is the tendency to look for information that supports one's preconceptions rather than information that could reject them; because such bias affects everyone, a systematic method rather than personal judgment is what keeps research objective.

Replication is the process of repeating research to determine the extent to which findings generalize across time and situations; a finding is more trustworthy when the same or similar results appear when the study is repeated, and exact replication copies the methods of the original study.
In the 2015 Open Science Collaboration effort, only about one-third of psychological studies drawn from prestigious journals replicated.

By the time information is accepted by the scientific community it has typically been tested repeatedly; non-replicating findings, revised hypotheses, and corrected conclusions are how science corrects itself.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The specific list of steps in the scientific method varies across sources: some textbooks name four steps, some name seven, and OpenStax Psychology 2e describes the process as a hypothesis-testing loop rather than a fixed step list.
positions: OpenStax Psychology 2e Section 2.1 describes the scientific method as a circular process in which hypotheses are derived from theories and tested, and theories are modified or refined based on results — without naming a fixed numbered list of steps.

Simply Psychology's Steps of the Scientific Method article names a sequence: make an observation, ask a question, form a hypothesis, run an experiment (gather data), analyze the data and draw conclusions, share your results, and repeat the method.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the steps as 'commonly taught' guidelines rather than a single canonical recipe, explicitly notes that the sequence is flexible and cyclical, and anchors the underlying mechanics (hypothesis → test → analyze → refine) in OpenStax's description of the hypothesis-testing loop.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The 2015 Open Science Collaboration replication estimate: media coverage sometimes misreads the roughly one-third replication rate as meaning a third of all psychology findings are false.
positions: Noba reports that only about 1/3 of the psychological studies in premier journals replicated in the 2015 effort, and that the problem is pronounced in social psychology (with cognitive psychology at about 53%).
Some popular summaries treat non-replication as evidence that psychology is unreliable.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the figure factually, attributes it to the Noba Project's account of the 2015 Open Science Collaboration project, and frames non-replication as part of the self-correcting process rather than as proof that psychology is broken.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, Section 2.1: Why Is Research Important?
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical OpenStax URL registered; read via Internet Archive capture (https://web.archive.org/web/2024/https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/2-1-why-is-research-important) because openstax.org blocks direct fetch. Supports: the definition of the scientific method as ideas tested against the real world through empirical observation, the hypothesis as a testable if-then prediction, falsifiability, empirical knowledge as the hallmark of scientific evidence, research as the difference between facts and opinions, and repeated testing before acceptance.

sourceRecords.title: The Replication Crisis in Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Module by Edward Diener and Robert Biswas-Diener (University of Utah / University of Virginia / Portland State University). Supports: the definition of replication as repeating research to determine how far findings generalize across time and situations, the definition of exact replication, the 2015 Open Science Collaboration finding that roughly one-third of studies from prestigious journals replicated, and the value of waiting for replications before treating a finding as established.

sourceRecords.title: Steps of the Scientific Method
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B educational reference, used sparingly as a secondary source. Supports the commonly taught step sequence (observation, question, hypothesis, experiment/data gathering, analysis and conclusions, sharing results, iteration), the claim that the steps are guidelines rather than a rigid sequence, empiricism as knowledge from direct observation rather than intuition or authority, falsifiability, and bias control as a reason for using a systematic method.

sourceRecords.title: Confirmation Bias in Psychology: Definition & Examples
sourceRecords.notes: Tier B educational reference. Provides the definition of confirmation bias as the tendency to look for information that supports, rather than rejects, one's preconceptions, explicitly attributing that definition to the American Psychological Association. Used only for the definition; the worked example and scenarios in the lesson are original.
